course_details.Overview of class: This course explores the evolution of Gospel music from its African roots to today's abundant sub-genres of contemporary Gospel. Through readings, videos, and live performances, students will engage in critical discussions regarding the language, expression, and social-historical implications of this original American art form. The class also looks at the lives of some of Gospel's luminaries, including Chicago's own Professor Thomas A. Dorsey, the "Father of Black Gospel Music."

course_name: Art and Performance in Asian America

course_info.course_name: Art and Performance in Asian America

course_details.Overview of class: What is Asian American art? How do the racial and political undercurrents of the designation "Asian American" lend itself to various stylized forms, such as the cyborg, alien, recluse, or Orient? In this class, we will examine a range of art objects and performances by Asian American and Asian diasporic artists—including but not limited to Mitski, Patty Chang, Yoko Ono and Jes Fan—which have emerged out of or in relation to the varied experiences and imaginaries of Asia/ America. Instead of pursing a comprehensive historiography of Asian American art, we turn our attention how these experiments—in video, photography, performance art, and music—elaborate the inconsistencies and resonances that permeate formations of Asia America. Finally, in locating our study at the intersection of Asian American studies and Performance studies, we will learn to lean into our senses (sight, touch, hearing) and the sensory (the visible, invisible, haptic, tactile, whispers, murmurs, screams, etc.) as analytical tools capable of complicating the association between identity and representation.

course_details.Overview of class: This course introduces students to performance research as an interdisciplinary field and method of inquiry. Students will explore performance practice as a mode of knowledge production across theater, performance art, dance, activism, and digital spaces. Through critical readings, embodied research labs, practice-based inquiry, and creative documentation, students will learn to analyze and generate research that employs performance as a modality of social exploration and critique. The course culminates in original performance-based research projects.

Explores AfroFuturism, a literary and cultural aesthetic demonstrating/imagining how people of color project ourselves into narratives of the future. Investigation of speculative fiction, fantasy literature, sound cultures, artworks, music videos, and dance to trace the concept of an AfroFuturist point of view. Creation of AfroFuturist media and performances. Artists considered include writers Samuel R. Delany and Andrea Hairston; musicians Parliament-Funkadelic and Sun Ra; filmmaker Hype Williams; performers Janelle Monae and Flying Lotus.

The course is arranged around disciplinary rhetorics of sound, literature, performance, and visual cultures. Together we will read several texts together and consider their contents and contexts. Creative exercises or writing exercises will be spread throughout the semester. At least one of these exercises should be executed in a small group, as demonstration of an ensemble of collective action and shared study. As a final offering, students will produce either a research paper of 15-20 pages length, or a performance/media object of significant complexity as a final outcome of coursework.
